### G136 - the Task 7 brief's "emit it and look at it" step cannot use the mechanism it names, and the eight drawings it produced instead were made by a SCRATCH harness that is not in the tree

The brief's Step 6 is *"Draw a block with each of the eight registered
templates and LOOK AT THE OUTPUT. Eight single-block fixture designs, emitted,
exported to PDF, converted, read with the Read tool."* The stated route is
`generate` then `exportPdf`. **Neither is in this repository**: `generate`
needs `layoutSheet` from `render/sheets.ts` and `exportPdf` lives in
`kicadRun.ts`, both Task 6b's (**G131** records the same obstruction for Task
6's identical step). The criterion - look at each template's output and say
what it looks like - was met by a different mechanism and the deviation is
recorded here rather than left implicit.

**What was done.** A throwaway harness in the session scratchpad builds one
block per registered template id from the ported tests' own fixtures, calls
`realiseBlock`, applies a rigid whole-grid translation so the drawing lands on
the paper, assembles a one-block `SheetDrawing` from ported functions only
(`anchorsToSymbols`, `blockFields`, `pinMarks`, `junctionPoints`,
`placedNoConnects`, `drawnBoxes`/`boundsOf`), hands it to the ported
`emitSheet`/`emitRoot`, and KiCad renders it. **The template decides every
position; the harness decides nothing but the offset and the frame box.**

**It is NOT committed, deliberately.** It would be a second sheet assembler
beside `render/sheets.ts`, which is the thing Task 6b ports, and this
repository's rule is that a superseded pattern is deleted rather than left for
somebody to find and trust. Anyone wanting to repeat the look should use
`layoutSheet` once it lands.

**What the eight look like**, read as PNGs at 170 dpi:

- **rail-row** - two 10k resistors hanging from a `3V3` power arrow on a
  shared top wire, each dropping to its own `SIG_A`/`SIG_B` global label.
  Reference and value right of each body. Clean.
- **decoupling-bank** - three capacitors in a row between a `3V3`/`VDDA` top
  and a `GND` bottom, the two `3V3` caps adjacent and `VDDA` given its own
  arrow. Rows split at every tap, so the junction dots sit where three ends
  meet and nowhere else.
- **divider** - R1 from `3V3` down to the tap, R2 to `GND`, C3 shunting the
  tap, the tap carried right to a `TAP` label. The three-piece tap row is
  visible as three segments with dots at the two interior attachments.
- **passive-chain** - the most convincing of the eight: a left-to-right line
  from a `TIP` label through R1, with C2 and D3 shunting down to `GND`, then
  C4 in series, then the parallel pair C6 over R5 drawn as a rectangle above
  the line, then C7 down to `GND`, a `T` label up, and R8 out to `VMID`.
  Reads like a hand-drawn input stage.
- **crystal** - Y1 vertical in the middle with pins 2 and 4 to `GND` above and
  below, pin 1 and pin 3 out to left and right, a load capacitor under each
  clock net and `HSE_IN`/`HSE_OUT` labels standing up. Symmetric.
- **connector-fanout** - J1 on the left with four pins fanning right; the two
  `DP` pins joined and taken to one label, `CC` through R2 to a `GND` glyph,
  pin 4 to its own `GND`. The join wire crosses `CC`'s stub without a dot,
  which is what the ported test asserts.
- **regulator** - U1 in the centre, `VIN` in from the left through C2, `VOUT`
  out to the right into C3 and C4, the NR capacitor standing above pin 4, EN
  strapped back to the input rail, GND down. Textbook.
- **opamp-stage** - the triangle with + above -, both inputs fed from the left
  through series chains, two `VMID` references above the + input, the feedback
  pair R6 over C7 drawn below the amplifier from - back to the output, and the
  output chain R10 to an `NS` label with C11 shunting to `GND`.

**ROUND 2 CORRECTS THREE THINGS IN THE PARAGRAPHS ABOVE, AND THEY MATTER
BECAUSE THESE EIGHT DESCRIPTIONS ARE THE FIRST LOOK ANYONE HAS HAD.**

**(a) "The harness decides nothing but the offset and the frame box" was a bad
way to put it, and it undercut a claim that is provable.** Those are not
nothing: they are precisely the two decisions whose real implementations exist
to prevent the collision described below. `render/frames.ts` exports
`frameSize`, whose comment reads *"Content box grown by two grid steps, title
band on top, wide enough for the band's text"* and which takes
`Math.max(content, text)` over a `bandHeight` of `(1 + legend.length) * LINE`,
and `contentOffset`, *"Grid-multiple offset putting the content inside a frame
at `at`, below the title band"*. The harness reserved **no band and no title
width**; it put the content at a flat margin and drew a box one grid step
around the extent with the title at the corner. **So the frame-title collision
is attributable to the harness, and that attribution is now evidence rather
than assertion.** What remains true is the thing that matters: the harness
chooses no symbol position, rotation or wire - the template does all of that.

**(b) THE HARNESS ALSO CHOSE WHICH FIXTURE EACH TEMPLATE DREW, AND ROUND 1 DID
NOT SAY SO.** The eight circuits are lifted from the ported template tests,
which are the pedals project's own fixtures for a dense digital mainboard -
**G87** records that the templates were sized by exactly that and that there
is NO evidence about how they behave on a discrete audio circuit. **So the
descriptions above are pictures of (template x pedals fixture), not of
templates drawing this repository's circuits.** *"The most convincing of the
eight"* and *"textbook"* are judgements about a fixture as much as about a
template, and **a reader must not take them as evidence of applicability** -
that is Task 10's census, a different measurement, and nothing here bears on
it.

**TASK 10 DID NOT FILL THE GAP (b) NAMES, AND HERE IS WHAT IT MEASURED ABOUT
WHY - CORRECTED IN ROUND 2 OF THAT TASK, BECAUSE ROUND 1's VERSION OF THIS
PARAGRAPH WAS WRONG FOR TWO NAMED BLOCKS.** It said *"no template draws any of
this repository's twelve declared blocks, so there is no (template x this
repository's block) drawing to describe"* and that **the MECHANISM below is not
sufficient**. **Both are false.** **G160**'s second column measures that
`connector-fanout`, given an anchor, draws **`tp-leg-lower-a` and
`tp-leg-lower-b`** - 3 placements, 4 wires, 3 anchors each, with `checkLayout`
clean inside the template.

**So the MECHANISM below IS sufficient for those two, and Task 12 is not needed
for them.** What blocks the look is exactly what this entry already says: this
repository has no sheet assembler, because `layoutSheet` is Task 6b's
(**G131**). When it lands, **`tp-leg-lower-a` and `tp-leg-lower-b` are the first
candidates** - the first *(template x this repository's circuit)* pictures
anybody can take, which is precisely what caveat (b) says nobody has looked at.

**What remains true of the other ten blocks.** `realiseBlock` refuses all 12 as
declared, every one needing the ELK backend; and the sweep finds **no registered
template that draws those ten under any anchor over any member unit**, so for
them a picture does need Task 12's backend and will be ELK's work rather than a
template's.

**(c) "`checkLayout` clean on all eight" is BLOCK-LEVEL ONLY, and weaker than
what the real pipeline runs.** `checkLayout` sees one block's placements,
wires and anchors. `layoutSheet` additionally runs `assertSheetSafe(scene)`
and `assertTextClear(textScene(…, { blocks, powers, labels, texts, frames }))`
over the whole sheet INCLUDING the frames
(`$SCHGEN_SOURCE/render/sheets.ts:126-127`). **Neither ran here**, because
both live in `render/sheetCheck.ts` and `render/textScene.ts`'s sheet entry
point, which is Task 6b's. The frame-title collision is exactly the class of
defect `assertTextClear` over a frame-bearing scene is there to catch, which
is the second half of why (a)'s attribution holds.

**(d) The per-template counts are not reproducible until `layoutSheet` lands.**
`opamp-stage: 11 symbols, 21 wires, 7 junctions` and its seven siblings came
from a harness that is not in the tree, so nobody can re-derive them without
writing one again. That is a known cost of not committing a second sheet
assembler, and the MECHANISM below is the fix.

**The two original caveats, unchanged.** The frame TITLE collides with the
topmost power symbol's text on four of the eight (`rail-row`,
`decoupling-bank`, `divider`, `crystal`): that is the harness putting the
title at the frame's top-left corner, **not a template defect** -
`render/frames.ts` is what places a title and it is not in this tree. And the
`checkLayout` that the drawings were measured against ran on the offset
layout, clean on all eight.

- **Found** 2026-10-19, Task 7, Step 6.

### G137 - **the round-1 premise of this entry was FALSE and is the finding**: a ported test's six-test skip is real but the suite-level backstop already exists, so the narrower gap is a reader of one file, and the `CI` fix was rejected for reasons worth recording

**ROUND 1 SAID THE BACKSTOP DOES NOT EXIST. IT DOES, AND THAT SENTENCE IS THE
ONE A LATER AGENT WOULD HAVE ACTED ON.** The original entry concluded *"six
tests disappear quietly and nothing fails"*. The second half is false.
`tests/schgen/render/stock-symbols.test.ts` is hand-written, calls
`stockSymbolDir()` directly, and its own doc comment says **"THESE DO NOT SKIP
WHEN KiCad IS ABSENT."** On a machine without KiCad's stock symbol libraries
**this repository's suite is already red**, so the cardinal sin - a skipped
check that looks like a passing one - is NOT live at suite level, and round
1's CRITERION was already met when it was written.

**What IS real, and it is narrower.**
`tests/schgen/render/templates/opamp-stock.kicad.test.ts` is ported and guards
its whole `describe` with `describe.skipIf(skipWithout(ready, "the KiCad stock
symbol library Amplifier_Operational"))`, where `ready` is
`fs.existsSync(path.join(stockSymbolDir(), "Amplifier_Operational.kicad_sym"))`.
**A reader running that one file on a machine without the library sees
`0 pass / 6 skip / 0 fail` and no explanation.** The suite as a whole would
still be red, from a different file, which that reader is not looking at.

**SETTLED, in a hand-written file, by asserting the ported file's own
predicate.** `tests/schgen/render/stock-symbols.test.ts` gained one test -
*"the stock op-amp library a ported test skips on is present, so that test did
not skip"* - which asserts exactly that `existsSync` and, when it fails, names
the ported file, says it SKIPPED its six tests, and says what to install. No
`cuts`, no edit to a ported file, no environment lie, and it binds for bare
`bun test` as well as for `make check`. House precedent: the same file's
existing tests already refuse rather than skip, for the reason
`tests/kicad/symbol-library-disk.ts` gives.

**THE `CI` MECHANISM ROUND 1 PROPOSED WAS REJECTED, AND WHY MATTERS MORE THAN
THAT IT WAS.** `skipWithout` throws when `CI` is set and the tool is missing,
so *"set `CI` in whatever invokes the suite"* looks like a free fix. Three
reasons not to, in order of weight:

1. **It cannot be seen to work on the machine that would adopt it.** With the
   library present, `skipWithout` returns `false` before it ever reads `CI`,
   so `bun test .../opamp-stock.kicad.test.ts` is **6 pass / 0 fail with and
   without `CI=true`** here. A fix whose effect is invisible wherever it is
   installed is a fix nobody can verify.
2. **It protects one entry point.** `package.json`'s script is a bare
   `"test": "bun test"`, which is what every task report in this plan actually
   runs; setting `CI` in `make check` would leave that path unguarded.
3. **It is an environment lie.** Asserting `CI` on a developer machine to buy
   one refusal is a false statement about the environment, bought for one call
   site: `process.env["CI"]` is read in exactly **one** place in the whole
   repository (`tests/schgen/__fixtures__/require-tool.ts:17`), so it has no
   other side effects today - but that is an argument that it is cheap, not
   that it is right, and the next thing to read `CI` would inherit the lie.

- **Found** 2026-10-19, Task 7, Step 3. **Round-1 premise corrected
  2026-10-19 at Task 7 review**, which checked the claim rather than
  believing it.
- **Evidence**, all driven, each a check that could have failed:
  - **The backstop fires.**
    `KICAD_CLI=/nonexistent/bin/kicad-cli bun test tests/schgen/render/stock-symbols.test.ts`
    -> **2 pass / 5 fail**. And the narrower case fires too: with
    `KICAD_SYMBOL_DIR` pointed at a temp directory holding only
    `Device.kicad_sym`, `symbolLibraries(["Amplifier_Operational"])` throws
    *"no symbol library for nickname(s) Amplifier_Operational. Looked in the
    installed stock directory …"*.
  - **The skip is real.** With the libraries present the ported file is
    **6 pass / 0 fail**; with `KICAD_CLI=/nonexistent/bin/kicad-cli` it is
    **0 pass / 6 skip / 0 fail**; with that plus `CI=true` it is
    **0 pass / 1 fail / 1 error**, the module-scope throw.
  - **`CI` is invisible here.** `CI=true bun test .../opamp-stock.kicad.test.ts`
    with the library present is **6 pass / 0 fail**, identical to the run
    without it.
  - **`CI` has one reader.** `grep -rn 'env\["CI"\]' lib tools tests` returns
    exactly one line, `tests/schgen/__fixtures__/require-tool.ts:17`.
  - **The new assertion has teeth.** With `KICAD_SYMBOL_DIR` pointed at the
    one-library temp directory, `stock-symbols.test.ts` is **4 pass / 4 fail**
    and the new test fails by name:
    *"…/Amplifier_Operational.kicad_sym is missing, so
    tests/schgen/render/templates/opamp-stock.kicad.test.ts SKIPPED its six
    tests rather than running them…"*. Restored, it is **8 pass / 0 fail**.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer ran every command above, wrote the new
  test and drove it both ways. The correction to round 1 was RELAYED by the
  Task 7 reviewer and then reproduced here in full before being written down.
- **Why it is open** the ported file still skips, and that is not fixable from
  this repository: a ported file may not be hand-edited and a `cuts` entry can
  only delete, so the `describe.skipIf` wrapper stays. What the new assertion
  buys is that the skip can no longer happen without something adjacent saying
  so by name. The residual is that the two live in different files and nothing
  ties them together but prose.
- **What would settle it** **CRITERION:** a skipped `opamp-stock.kicad.test.ts`
  cannot occur without a check failing and naming it. That is met today.
  **The remaining, narrower CRITERION:** the tie between the ported file's
  `ready` expression and the hand-written assertion of it survives a change to
  either. **MECHANISM**, untried: have the ported file's predicate exported
  from somewhere both can import - which needs a change in the pedals source,
  not here - or assert the ported file's own source text contains the
  expression, which is a grep and weaker than it looks. **NOT the mechanism:
  setting `CI`**, for the three reasons above.

### G138 - three signatures in the Task 7 brief's `Produces` block do not match the source it says they are unchanged from, and one names a type that does not exist

The brief states its `Produces` block is *"unchanged from the source - Task 8
is what widens it"*. Checked against
`$SCHGEN_SOURCE/render/` line by line, three entries differ. None is a defect
in the port - the ported files carry the source's signatures verbatim - but a
later task reading the plan rather than the code would widen the wrong thing.

| the brief says | the source has | where |
|---|---|---|
| `planStage(g: BlockSubgraph): StagePlanResult` | `planStage(g: BlockSubgraph): Planned` | `render/templates/opampClassify.ts:102` |
| `tracePaths(g, unit, skip: ReadonlySet<NetName>)` | `tracePaths(g, anchor, skip: ReadonlySet<PinNumber>)` | `render/fanoutKit.ts:52` |
| `fanout(g, unit, rot, paths: readonly Path[])` | `fanout(g, anchor, rot, paths: readonly OutwardPath[])` | `render/fanoutKit.ts:209` |

**`StagePlanResult` does not exist anywhere in the source tree**
(`grep -rn StagePlanResult $SCHGEN_SOURCE/` returns nothing); the exported
type is `Planned`. The brief's Step 5 repeats the wrong name when it lists the
five helper result types Task 8 must widen, so the error is in two places in
one document. `skip` being keyed by `PinNumber` rather than `NetName` is the
sharper of the other two: a reader planning Task 8's classification from the
brief would have the wrong idea of what a fan-out skips.

Everything else in the block checks out: `Template`, `RealiseResult`,

`realiseBlock`, `ladder`, `chain` and `commonRailLadder` match the source
exactly, and the eight registered ids are the eight the brief names.

### G139 - the port manifest has a third category, `diverged`, and **26 of its 90 files now re-derive from nothing** - nine of them ported TESTS, and a tenth the fixture they share

**What was done.** `tools/schgen/port-manifest.json` gained a `diverged` list
beside `files` and `handWritten`. An entry is
`{ from, to, task, why }`: the pedals source it was ported from, where it
lives, which task diverged it, and why.
`tests/schgen/port-fidelity.test.ts` holds three new claims, each of which can
fail - `from` exists under `$SCHGEN_SOURCE`, `to` exists on disk, `task` and
`why` are non-empty - plus disjointness of the three categories, and the
bidirectional `lib/schgen/` completeness check now unions all three rather
than two. `tools/schgen/port.ts` prints one `DIVERGED, not rewritten:` line
per entry on every run, and `resolveSpecifier` resolves `@/schgen/<path>`
imports through `diverged` as well as `files`, because a diverged file still
occupies its destination and the files importing it are still ports.

**Why a third category rather than deleting the entries.** Task 8 widens
`RealiseResult` from two outcomes to five across `render/block-types.ts`, the
seven templates and five helper modules, and deletes the `labels` rendering
(plan decision **D3**, **G140**) that the pedals source has and will keep.
**`cuts` cannot express either**: a cut is deletion-only and both are
modifications. Dropping the manifest entries would have destroyed each file's
provenance and left nothing recording that it ever was a port or what of -
which is the shape of failure this plan has rejected twice. Controller ruling
**R18** states the criterion met here: a file may diverge, and it may not
diverge silently.

**THE COST, WHICH IS NOT SMALL AND IS THE REASON THIS ENTRY EXISTS.** Nothing
compares a diverged file against its source again. An upstream fix in
`digital-pedal-platform` will not arrive by re-running the porter; a drift
between the two is invisible to every check in this repository; and the `cuts`
a file carried while it was ported stop being declared anywhere but this
manifest's git history. **Measured after Task 8: `files[]` holds 64 entries,
`diverged` 26 and `handWritten` 10**, so a little over a quarter of what was
ported is no longer checked against anything. **Nine of the twenty-six are
ported TESTS** - eight of them from the `labels` deletion, plus
`render/templates/passiveChain.test.ts` from the type widening - including the
four MCU-cut carriers
(`ir/build.test.ts` with nine cut entries, `ir/classify.test.ts`,
`ir/validate.test.ts`, `render/templates/opampStock.kicad.test.ts`) and the
ported fixture `__fixtures__/circuits.ts`. **Five of the nine are rows of
**G124**'s table** - the port-parity work Task 7 landed or unblocked
(`render/templates/passiveChain.test.ts`,
`render/templates/opampStock.kicad.test.ts`, `render/textClearance.test.ts`,
`render/unitText.test.ts`, `render/noConnectEnds.test.ts`); the other four
came in with Tasks 2, 4 and 6. All nine still RUN, and their assertions are
unchanged except the twelve in `passiveChain.test.ts` that this task's
widening required and that got STRONGER (they now pin the mismatch kind).
What is gone is the byte-check that would have caught a drift in what they
assert.

**THE ALTERNATIVE MECHANISM, CONSIDERED AND NOT TAKEN, BECAUSE A LATER PORT
TASK MAY WANT IT.** A `replacements` list on a `files[]` entry -
`{ text, with, occurrences }`, validated exactly as `cuts` is and applied the
same way - would be a generalisation of `cuts` that covers a *mechanical,
local* substitution, keeping a file in `files[]` and byte-checked.

**ROUND 1 REJECTED IT ON A LOAD-BEARING SENTENCE THAT IS FALSE, AND THE ENTRY
WRITTEN IN THE SAME COMMIT DISPROVES IT.** It said *"every one of the nine
diverged test files needs only `{ kind: "labels", reason: X }` to become
`{ kind: "bus", groups: [] }`, which is 17 sites of pure substitution"*. **It
is not one substitution and the nine were never mechanically divergeable**:

- **G140**, written in the same commit, records that **16 sites go to
  `{kind: "bus", groups: []}` and one to `{kind: "auto"}`**, and that the split
  was *measured* - with `bus` in `ir/validate.test.ts` the `renderings` rule
  adds *"net X is in no bus group"* to every assertion in the file. A
  text-substitution rule cannot make that choice; a person had to.
- The `reason:` strings differ site by site (`"test"`, `"t"`, `"fixture"`,
  `"fixture peer"`, `"fixture: unused op-amp units"`), so the 17 sites are not
  17 instances of one rule either.
- `ir/classify.test.ts` needed a test RENAMED (*"labels every net of a
  labels-rendered block"* → *"bus-rendered"*), which is not a substitution of
  the construction at all.
- `render/text-clearance.test.ts` needed an **unrelated** change in the same
  file - `FieldScene.scope` → `block` - which belongs to the widening, not to
  D3, and which no `labels` rule would have covered.

So the honest ground for rejecting `replacements` is the first one only, and it
stands on its own: **it puts new program text inside a JSON manifest**,
reviewable for a one-liner and unreviewable at any scale, with a line between
the two that every future agent would redraw. The second ground round 1 gave -
that the pedals source keeps `labels` permanently, so the copies are *intended*
to differ - is true and is why a rewrite rule would have had to encode the
intent anyway; it does not hold for the type widening, where the pedals source
may well widen the same way later. **That is exactly why `sourceSha` was taken
up instead** (below): it is the one mechanism that covers all 26 files,
including the thirteen `lib/` files the second ground does not reach.

- **Found** 2026-10-19, Task 8, Step 4, as the obstruction ruling R18
  anticipated.
- **Evidence** checks that could have failed, and two that did:

  - **A WRONG `from` FAILS.** The provenance assertion is not decorative:

- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer added the category, ran the porter,

**THE CRITERION WAS UNENFORCED FOR NINE OF THE 26 ENTRIES, WHICH ROUND 1

**Three checks were added in review, under the reviewer's extension of R18**

1. **Completeness over `tests/schgen/` as well as `lib/schgen/`**, both arms

2. **No `handWritten` path may shadow a pedals source file.** `[RAN]`

3. **`sourceSha` per `diverged` entry** - SHA-256 of the pedals file as it stood

   Tampering with one hash fails naming the file and printing both hashes. It is

- **Why it is open** the loss is reduced, not closed. `sourceSha` detects that
  the source moved and can say nothing about whether this repository's copy
  should take the change; and the 26 copies here still drift freely, checked by

- **What would settle it** **CRITERION:** a drift between a diverged file and
  its pedals source is detectable by a check in this repository, rather than

  half that detects upstream movement, and it covers all 26 files. The other

### G140 - the `labels` rendering is DELETED from the port, which is a deliberate deviation from *port whole*, and it took a validation rule and a ported test with it

`Rendering` in the pedals source has three variants: `wired`, `bus` and
`{ kind: "labels"; reason: string }`, the last of which draws a block's
connectivity entirely in net labels. **Task 8 deletes it and adds
`{ kind: "auto" }`**, per plan decision **D3**. This is recorded here because
the plan's governing posture is to port whole and fix in a later task with a
stated reason, and this is that stated reason.

**The reasons, which are three entries in this file pointing the same way.**
**G84** records the pedals design review that killed the labels fallback
there - *"Why generate a knowingly inferior schematic and rely on an agent
later noticing it? … You already know the desired invariant. Make the tooling
enforce it"* - and its finding that the cost of a fallback is paid by the
**gate**, not merely by the drawing. **G81** records that this repository's
own `lib/kicad/schematic.ts` *"emits the exact pathology another project was
blocked from shipping"*: every pin on a short wire to a net label,
connectivity entirely in labels. Task 19 deletes that emitter. Porting a
second labels-everywhere renderer in the programme that deletes the first
would be absurd.

**WHAT WENT WITH IT, AND THE SECOND ITEM IS THE ONE A LATER READER WOULD
MISS.**

1. `ir/validate.ts`'s `renderings` rule loses its one-line clause
   *"block `<id>`: labels rendering needs a reason"*. That is a pure
   deletion, so it is a declared `cuts` entry in the port manifest, and
   `ir/validate.ts` stays in `files[]` and stays byte-checked.
2. **The ported test that exercised that rule is DELETED** -
   `tests/schgen/ir/validate.test.ts`'s *"V6: requires a reason for label
   rendering"*. It asserted a message nothing can now produce. Supersede
   means delete, so it is gone rather than skipped or stubbed, and a comment
   stands where it was naming this entry. **It is NOT an R4 deferral**: there
   is no later task that re-adds it, because the rule it tested does not
   exist in this repository any more.
3. `report.ts`'s "Label-rendered blocks" section is now "Automatically
   rendered blocks", listing the `auto` blocks - the ones whose drawing
   nobody declared - and there is no reason string to print, because
   `{ kind: "auto" }` carries no payload.
4. **Twelve ported files diverge for this** and are listed in `diverged`;
   **G139** has the count and the cost.

**AND THE SUBSTITUTION IN THE FIXTURES IS A DECISION, NOT A FIND-AND-REPLACE.**
Seventeen sites in nine ported test files and the ported fixture declared
`{ kind: "labels", reason: X }`. Sixteen are now `{ kind: "bus", groups: [] }`
and one is `{ kind: "auto" }`, and the split is forced:

- `bus` is the behavioural equal of `labels` for everything those fixtures
  measure. `labelledNets` labels every net of a `bus` block (and
  `tests/schgen/ir/single-pin-net-guard.test.ts` already used
  `{ kind: "bus", groups: [] }` for exactly that), and
  `valuesAlong(rendering)` returns `true` for `bus` as it did for `labels`,
  which decides whether a power symbol's value runs along its glyph - so a
  careless `auto` here would have silently moved the text that
  `render/text-clearance.test.ts`, `unit-text.test.ts`,
  `no-connect-ends.test.ts` and `drawn-text.test.ts` exist to measure.
- `tests/schgen/ir/validate.test.ts` is the exception and had to be `auto`:
  every spec in that file must validate CLEAN apart from the rule under test,
  and the `renderings` rule requires every non-rail net of a `bus` block to be
  in exactly one group - so `{ kind: "bus", groups: [] }` would have added
  *"net X is in no bus group"* to **every** assertion in the file, including
  two `toEqual` ones. `auto` has no rule of its own.

- **Found** 2026-10-19, Task 8, Step 8.
- **Evidence** `bun run typecheck` clean and `bun test tests/schgen/` at
  **337 pass / 0 fail at commit `e5dd445`** with `labels` absent from
  `Rendering` (the count is that commit's and is not reproducible later - the
  same command is 362 across 45 files by the end of Task 8, since the task
  adds test files; stamping the commit is what makes it checkable) - a check
  that could have failed at 17 sites and at every `switch` over the union, and
  the `switch` in `report.ts` is exhaustive with no `default`, so an unhandled
  `auto` is a compile error rather than a silent `undefined`. The `bus`/`auto`
  split above was derived by reading `valuesAlong` (`render/power-text.ts`)
  and the `renderings` rule (`ir/validate.ts`), and the `auto` choice for
  `validate.test.ts` was **measured, not reasoned**: with `bus` there, the
  file fails.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer made the deletion, ran both, and read
  the two rules the substitution turns on.
- **Why it is open** it is a permanent, deliberate divergence from the pedals
  source that a later porter needs to know about before touching
  `Rendering` or any fixture that declares one. It is not a defect.
- **What would settle it** nothing settles the deviation; what it is held to
  is a standing **CRITERION: no generated schematic from this repository
  carries a block's connectivity only in labels, and no path produces a
  knowingly inferior drawing** - a block no template realises fails
  generation naming the block (**G84**'s criterion, which this implements).
  **MECHANISM, in two halves, neither finished at this commit:** Step 7 of
  this same task writes `selectRenderer` to refuse on any mismatch that is not
  `not-applicable` and to fall to ELK only when every template reports one;
  the other half is Task 19's deletion of `lib/kicad/schematic.ts`, which is
  the thing in this repository that actually draws that way today.

### G141 - measured: **four of the eight templates can never apply to an `auto` block**, because the anchor they need lives on the `wired` variant

`{ kind: "auto" }` carries no payload, by decision **D3**. Four templates read
their anchor as `const anchor = r.kind === "wired" ? r.anchor : null` -
`connector-fanout`, `crystal`, `regulator` and `opamp-stage` (the last through
`planStage`) - and each refuses immediately when it is null:
*"connector-fanout needs an anchor"*, *"crystal needs an anchor with roles a
and b"*, *"regulator needs an anchor with roles in and out"*, *"opamp-stage
needs an anchor with roles out, inv and noninv"*. All four of those refusals
are `not-applicable`.

**So an `auto` block is in practice offered four templates, not eight**:
`rail-row`, `decoupling-bank`, `divider` and `passive-chain`, the four that
read only the subgraph. An op-amp stage, a regulator, a crystal or a connector
fan-out declared `auto` therefore reaches **ELK** - every template reports
`not-applicable`, which is exactly the condition that selects it - rather than
the template that was written for its idiom.

**This is not a defect in Task 8's selection rule**, which does what §1.3
says; and it is not obviously wrong, since those four templates genuinely
cannot be driven without knowing which pin is which. **What it means is that
`auto` cannot be used to say "work out which idiom this is"** for half the
template set, and a later task that expects it to will find the block going to
ELK silently - `{kind:"elk"}` is a selection, not a refusal, so nothing says
so out loud.

**MEASURED ON THIS REPOSITORY'S OWN BLOCKS, 2026-10-20, BY TASK 10's CENSUS.**
The consequence above was inferred from a five-pin regulator fixture; **G160**
now measures it where it matters. All **12** declared blocks of the four parity
circuits are `{kind:"auto"}` with `anchor: null`, and **48 of the census's 96
(block x template) verdicts are these four refusals** - one per anchor-driven
template per block, verbatim. The prediction in the paragraph above is confirmed
on named blocks: `ob-buffer`, `oc-audio` and `oc-sidechain` are op-amp stages
that reach ELK, and `opamp-stage` declines each with *"needs an anchor with roles
out, inv and noninv"*. **The third mechanism below is now PARTLY DONE**: the
census records which blocks reached ELK and which templates declined them, with
each sentence verbatim, in `docs/schematic/template-parity.md` - but as a
measurement tool, **not** in the render report a generated schematic carries, so
the silence this entry describes is still silent inside the pipeline. **The
criterion is not met**: no anchor is derivable from a subgraph today.

**AND ROUND 2 OF TASK 10 MEASURES WHAT THIS ENTRY'S FIRST MECHANISM WOULD BUY,
WHICH IS SMALL.** `tools/schgen/anchor-sweep.ts` brute-forces every anchor a
classifier could possibly choose - every member unit of every declared block,
every injective assignment of the template's roles to that unit's pins, **4664
probes** - and finds **2 realised**: `connector-fanout` on `tp-leg-lower-a` and
`tp-leg-lower-b`. **So "move the anchor off `wired`" or "infer the roles from
the subgraph" is worth at most 2 of 12 blocks**, not half the template set, and
that ceiling is measured rather than estimated. It also makes the consequence
concrete in the other direction: **for 10 of the 12 blocks the anchor is not what
is missing.**

- **Found** 2026-10-19, Task 8, Step 7, while building the selection test's
  "no template fits" fixture.
- **Evidence** `grep -n 'r.kind === "wired" ? r.anchor : null'
  lib/schgen/render/templates/*.ts` returns **four** lines, one per template:

  ```
  lib/schgen/render/templates/connector-fanout.ts:34
  lib/schgen/render/templates/opamp-classify.ts:139
  lib/schgen/render/templates/crystal.ts:67
  lib/schgen/render/templates/regulator.ts:186
  ```

  The `opamp-classify.ts` one is inside `planStage`, which `opamp-stage.ts`
  calls as its first statement, so it is `opamp-stage`'s anchor read rather
  than a fifth template's. The consequence is exercised: the selection test's
  `auto` fixture is a five-pin regulator part with its NR capacitor, and
  `selectRenderer` returns `{kind:"elk"}` for it - a check that would fail if
  any anchor-driven template had applied.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer ran the grep, read the four sites, and
  wrote the test that depends on the conclusion.
- **Why it is open** it is a limit of the new `auto` variant that nothing in
  the tree states, and Tasks 9, 10 and 15 are written against the
  post-Task-8 shape of `Rendering`.
- **What would settle it** **CRITERION:** a block that an idiom template
  would have drawn is not sent to ELK merely because its rendering declared
  no anchor - either the anchor is derivable from the subgraph, or the block
  is told so. **MECHANISM, untried, and two of them disagree:** either move
  the anchor off `wired` so `auto` can carry one, or have each anchor-driven
  template infer its roles from the subgraph (which is a classifier, not a
  template, and is the shape **G90** says gets expensive). A third, cheapest
  option is neither: have the render report say which blocks reached ELK and
  which templates declined them, so the silence is at least recorded.

### G142 - `valuesAlong` now returns `true` for `auto`, and its doc comment still says "the bus and labels renderers" - a stale sentence in a file that is deliberately NOT diverged

`render/power-text.ts`'s `valuesAlong(rendering)` is
`return rendering.kind !== "wired"`, documented as *"true for the bus and
labels renderers, whose anchors are pin stubs one pin pitch apart (horizontal
values of adjacent up/down symbols would overprint each other); wired
templates space their anchors for horizontal values."*

Task 8 deletes `labels` and adds `auto` (**G140**), so that function now
returns `true` for `auto` **and the comment names a renderer that no longer
exists**. Two separate things are wrong with that, and only one of them is
cosmetic:

1. The sentence is stale prose in a ported file.
2. **Whether an `auto` block's power values should run along their glyphs is
   undecided.** The reason the comment gives is about anchor SPACING - stubs
   one pitch apart overprint - and an ELK-laid block's anchor spacing is
   whatever ELK produced, which is neither the bus renderer's pitch nor a
   template's deliberate spacing. `true` is therefore a guess that happens to
   be the conservative one (along-values overprint less), not a decision.

**`power-text.ts` was deliberately left PORTED.** It is not in the Task 8
brief's file list, it still compiles and behaves, and diverging it would cost
its byte-check (**G139**) to fix a comment. **Recording it rather than
drifting it is the choice**, and this entry is the record.

### G143 - measured: all thirty template refusal sites classified, and the split is **18 / 2 / 1 / 0 with nine forwards** - one kind has no site at all and one has exactly one

Task 8's substance was reading each of the 30 `mismatch(reason)` sites and
saying which of four kinds it is. The result, per module, as the census now
pins it:

| module | not-applicable | invalid-geometry | clearance | backend-raised | forward | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `connector-fanout.ts` | 1 | 0 | **1** | 0 | 1 | 3 |
| `crystal.ts` | 5 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 6 |
| `divider.ts` | 6 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 6 |
| `opamp-stage.ts` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| `passive-chain.ts` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| `rail-row.ts` | 3 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 5 |
| `regulator.ts` | 3 | **2** | 0 | 0 | 3 | 8 |
| **total** | **18** | **2** | **1** | **0** | **9** | **30** |

**THE DISTRIBUTION IS THE FINDING, AND IT IS LOPSIDED ENOUGH TO BE WORTH
RECORDING.** Twenty-seven of the thirty are, directly or through a forward,
*"this block is not that idiom"*. **Exactly three sites in the whole template
set report a defect in something a template DREW**: `regulator.ts`'s two tie
checks and `connector-fanout.ts`'s rotation search. Every other refusal fires
before a part is placed.

**What that means for the selection rule.** §1.3's asymmetry - `not-applicable`
may select another renderer, anything else refuses - is doing its work on three
sites out of thirty. It is still the right rule (**G84**), but a reader should
not imagine the two arms are of comparable size: **the refusing arm is three
sites, and if any one of them were misclassified as `not-applicable` the whole
protection would be a third gone.** That is why the census pins the per-kind
counts and not only the total.

**`backend-raised` has no site, by design.** No template raises on its own
behalf. `render/blocks.ts` builds that kind when a template THROWS - which is
how the ~12 `throw new Error("unreachable: ...")` and symbol-lookup failures in
the template set now arrive - and the ELK backend will build it for the elkjs
crash **G94** measured.

**AND THE HELPER TYPES CARRY FAR MORE REFUSALS THAN THE CENSUS COUNTS**, which
is a scope statement rather than a defect: `classifyChain` alone has nine,
`tracePaths` eight, `planStage` about fourteen, and all of them are
`not-applicable`. They reach a caller through the nine forwards. So the honest
summary is: **the template set refuses in roughly sixty places and three of
them are about geometry.**

- **Found** 2026-10-19, Task 8, Step 6, by reading all thirty sites.
- **Evidence** two independent counts that agree, which is the only reason to
  believe either. (1) The per-site table above, written by reading each site
  and its surrounding control flow - recorded in full in the Task 8 report with
  the reason for each. (2) `tests/schgen/render/templates/mismatch-census.test.ts`,
  rewritten to extract the sites from the source text per module AND per kind,
  which reports exactly these numbers. A check that could have failed, and did:
  the first run of the extractor returned 23 `not-applicable` and 12 forwards,
  because its patterns also matched the HELPER result constructors
  (`notLadder`, `notBanked`, `refuse`) and `opamp-classify.ts`'s forwards into
  `Planned` - which are refusals but not `RealiseResult` ones. Narrowing it to
  the four exported constructors, with the forward pattern gated on a module
  that declares a `Template`, gave the table above.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer classified each site, wrote the
  extractor, and reconciled the two counts.
- **Why it is open** it is a measurement a later task needs and cannot
  re-derive cheaply: Task 12's backend and Task 14's error handling are both
  written against how often each kind actually occurs.
- **What would settle it** nothing - it is a measurement, not a defect. What

### G145 - the clearance mismatch's obstacle pair is recovered from `checkLayout`'s problem TEXT, not from a restructured `checkLayout`, and this is a deviation from the brief's stated mechanism

The Task 8 brief, on the one `clearance` site: *"It must name the constraint
and the obstacle pair, which means `checkLayout`'s problem strings need enough
structure for the pair to be recovered."* The obvious reading is to restructure
`checkLayout` so a problem is an object carrying its two obstacles. **That was
not done, and the reason is a count.**

`checkLayout` composes eleven sub-checks across **eight** ported modules -
`body-clearance.ts`, `text-scene.ts`, `glyph-clearance.ts`, `wire-safety.ts`,
`connectivity.ts`, `field-placement.ts`, `unit-pins.ts` and `layout-check.ts`
itself - every one of which returns `string[]`, and the clearance tests under
`tests/schgen/render/` assert that text verbatim. Restructuring it would have
diverged eight more ported files (**G139**) and rewritten the assertions of the
tests that hold them, which ruling **R4** forbids.

**What was done instead.** A new hand-written
`lib/schgen/render/problem-obstacles.ts` declares the structure the strings
already have: fifteen infix relation phrases plus one prefix form
(`bodies of A and B overlap`), **each transcribed from the function that writes
it and citing it**, and `obstaclesOf(problem)` splits a problem into its
relation and its two obstacles. `connector-fanout` passes that pair to
`clearanceViolation`, using the relation as the `constraint`.

**IT REFUSES RATHER THAN GUESSING, AND THAT IS THE PART THAT MATTERS.** Most
`checkLayout` problems name ONE subject - *"unit R1#1 is not placed"*, *"net N
is split into 2 pieces"* - and a few name three. `obstaclesOf` returns `null`
for anything whose relation it does not hold, and `connector-fanout` then
**throws**, naming the problem and the file to add the phrase to. An invented
pair would be a classification nobody can check, in the field a reader would
trust most. `selectRenderer` turns that throw into a `backend-raised` mismatch,
so the block is still refused - loudly, and never silently drawn.

**AND ROUND 1 OF THIS MODULE RETURNED A PLAUSIBLE-AND-WRONG PAIR FOR A
PRODUCER IT LISTED BY NAME, WHICH IS THE FAILURE THE PARAGRAPH ABOVE CLAIMS IT
PREVENTS.** Found in review. `componentProblems` (`layout-check.ts:128`) writes
`` `not-connected pin ${nc.what} touches ${whats(others)}` ``, and `whats`
joins **every** other item in the component with `", "`. The `" touches "`
relation had it, so with two or more others `obstacles[1]` came out as
`"wire 3 of B, wire 4 of B"` - **a list in a field documented as one obstacle**,
which Task 12 onward reads - and a **connectivity** defect (a pin declared not
connected is touching something) was filed as a `clearance` violation with
`constraint: "touches"`. Reachable: `connector-fanout` passes rotation 0's
FIRST problem whatever it is. **The relation's own citation named
`componentProblems` as one of its writers while the code mishandled it**, so
the module documented the gap it had. Fixed by a declared `NOT_A_PAIR` list,
checked before the relations, with its own citation and its own tests -
matching a relation is necessary and **not sufficient**.

**WHAT IT COSTS.** The pair is recovered by matching text, so a producer that
rewords its message stops being recognised, and nothing fails until a layout
actually collides that way: **the failure mode is a `backend-raised` refusal
where a `clearance` one was meant**, which is loud but misclassified.

**The mitigation is now a check rather than a convention.** Round 1 said the
mitigation was *"the citation list - every phrase names its writer, so the
claim is checkable by grep"*, which is a thing a person could do and nothing
did. Seven of the fifteen phrases have no asserted example (every example is a
transcription, and transcribing fifteen is fifteen chances to transcribe
wrongly), so **the test now asserts that each phrase OCCURS in the module its
citation names**. `[RAN]` Repointing `" lies under "`'s citation at
`wire-safety.ts` fails with *"`" lies under "` occurs in none of the modules
its citation names (wire-safety.ts)"*; restored. **The residual is narrower and
real**: occurrence does not establish that the phrase is written in the message
sense rather than appearing in a comment, and a producer that rewords its
message AND keeps the old wording in a comment would still pass.

- **Found** 2026-10-19, Task 8, Step 6.
- **Evidence** `tests/schgen/render/problem-obstacles.test.ts`, seven tests
  over problem strings transcribed from the producers, including the two
  ordering cases that could silently be wrong (`" lies on "` is a substring of
  `" lies on pin end "`, `" ends on "` of `" ends mid-wire on "`) and eight
  real one-subject problems that must return `null`. One of its strings -
  `"label A at (31.75, -5.08) overlaps body of J_USB#1"` - is the shape the
  ported `connector-fanout.test.ts` asserts through the real pipeline, so at
  least one example is held to the pipeline by a second test. **A check that
  could have failed and did:** two of its expectations were wrong on the first
  run, both about where a producer prints the coordinate, and the rule that cut
  a trailing ` at (x, y)` was removed because `body-clearance.ts` prints it on
  the LEFT of the relation and `wire-safety.ts` on the right - so cutting it
  from the second obstacle only would have stripped half the pairs.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer wrote the module and its test, read
  every producer's message format, and ran the suite.
- **Why it is open** the deviation is permanent unless `checkLayout` is
  restructured, and the misclassification risk above is real and unguarded.
- **What would settle it** **CRITERION:** a clearance refusal's obstacle pair
  is derived from the data the check had, not from the sentence it wrote - or,
  failing that, a reworded producer message fails a check in this repository
  rather than silently becoming unrecognisable. **MECHANISMS, both untried:**
  give `checkLayout` a structured sibling that returns
  `{ text, obstacles }` and let the string form be derived from it, which is a
  task of its own because eight modules produce those strings; or assert each
  declared relation against a problem produced by the real check rather than
  against a transcription, which is cheaper and catches a rewording.

### G146 - `realiseBlock`'s ELK backend parameter DEFAULTS to null, which is a deviation from the brief's signature, taken to keep nine ported test files byte-checked

The brief's `Produces` block states
`realiseBlock(c: Circuit, id: BlockId, symbols: SymbolResolver, elk: Backend | null)`.
As written, the fourth parameter is required. **Nine ported test files call
`realiseBlock(c, "B", symbols)` with three arguments** - the eight template
tests (`connector-fanout`, `crystal`, `divider`, `opamp-stage`,
`opamp-stock.kicad`, `passive-chain`, `rail-row`, `regulator`) and
`render/body-clearance.test.ts` - so a required parameter would have diverged
all nine (**G139**) to add the word `null`. Two of them diverge for other
reasons in this task anyway, so the marginal cost would have been **seven**
port-parity test files Task 7 landed.

`elk` therefore defaults to `null`. The type is what the brief says; what
deviates is that a caller may omit it.

**THIS IS NOT A FALLBACK, AND THE DISTINCTION IS WORTH STATING PRECISELY.** A
`wired` block never consults the backend - its template draws it or the block
is refused. An `auto` block whose every template reported `not-applicable`
reaches `elkLayout`, and with a null backend that **throws**, naming the block,
saying the backend is Task 12's fourth argument, and saying why it is not
defaulted: *"the alternative to a backend here is a knowingly inferior drawing,
which this generator does not produce - see docs/known-gaps.md G84."* Nothing
is skipped and nothing second-best is drawn.

**What the default does cost** is that a future caller can forget the argument
and not find out until it renders an `auto` block. There are no `auto` blocks
in this repository yet, so today that is a latent cost rather than a live one.

- **Found** 2026-10-19, Task 8, Step 7.
- **Evidence** `grep -rln 'realiseBlock' tests/` prints **ten** files, nine of
  which call it (the tenth, `render/realise-result.test.ts`, only names it in a
  comment), and `grep -rn 'realiseBlock(' tests/ | grep -c 'symbols)'` prints
  **49** - every one a three-argument call. With the parameter required,
  `bun run typecheck` fails once per call site. The
  refusal path is real rather than asserted: during Task 8 a mis-stated
  selection rule sent 43 of those very tests down it, and every one reported
  *"block B: every template reported \"not-applicable\", so this block needs
  the ELK backend, and realiseBlock was called without one"* - the throw doing
  exactly what it claims, on real circuits.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer wrote both, and read the 43 failures
  that proved the throw fires.
- **Why it is open** it is a deviation from a stated interface that Task 12
  and everything after it implements against.
- **What would settle it** **CRITERION:** no caller of `realiseBlock` can
  reach the ELK path without having decided what backend to use. **MECHANISM,
  untried:** make the parameter required in the task that lands the backend,
  by which time the ten test files are being touched for other reasons anyway;
  a weaker alternative is a lint that forbids a three-argument call outside
  `tests/`.

### G147 - **the plan contradicts itself about the selection rule: decision D3 scopes it to `auto` and Step 7 restates it unscoped**, and the unscoped reading turned 43 tests red by replacing declared templates with ELK

The Task 8 brief's Step 7: *"`wired` runs its declared template; `auto` tries
`TEMPLATES` in registered order; **all `not-applicable` → `{kind:"elk"}`; any
other mismatch → `{kind:"refused"}`**."* Implemented exactly that way,
`selectRenderer` sends a **wired** block whose declared template reports
`not-applicable` to the ELK backend.

`[RAN]` **43 tests went red in one run**, every one of them a refusal a
declared template was expected to produce. Each reported the same thing
instead:

```
block B: every template reported "not-applicable", so this block needs the ELK
backend, and realiseBlock was called without one.
```

where the ported test expected, for instance,
`template divider cannot realise its subgraph: parts to GND start from
different nodes (B, A)`.

**THE RULE IS ASYMMETRIC BECAUSE THE TWO RENDERINGS MAKE DIFFERENT CLAIMS.**
`{ kind: "wired", template: "divider" }` is an author asserting *this block is
drawn by the divider template*. The template answering *"this is not a
divider"* means the assertion is false, and that is a generation error naming
the block and the template - which is **G84**'s criterion in terms. `auto`
asserts nothing about which idiom fits, so every template declining it is
information rather than contradiction, and ELK is the next renderer rather than
a rescue. **Sending a wired block to a general router because its declared
template declined it is precisely the silent degradation G84 exists to
prevent**, and it would have been undeclared as well: the render report would
have said `wired` while ELK drew it.

**AND THIS IS A FAITHFUL READING OF THE GOVERNING DOCUMENTS RATHER THAN AN
IMPLEMENTER'S REFINEMENT OF THEM, WHICH ROUND 1 OF THIS ENTRY FAILED TO SAY.**
Round 1 rested the whole case on the 43 red tests - which is evidence that the
unscoped rule is wrong, and not an argument about what the rule IS. Three
licenses, and the third is the one that settles it:

1. **§1.3's ELK row quantifies over the LIBRARY, not over one template**: *"no
   template **in the library** supports this topology → route the block through
   ELK."* A `wired` block consults exactly one template, so a single
   `not-applicable` **never establishes §1.3's precondition for the ELK
   route**. The unscoped reading is the one that departs from §1.3.
2. **§1.3 has no row at all for "a declared template does not apply."** Its
   refusing row is *a template **supports** this topology and did not realise
   it acceptably*. Wired-not-applicable is a fourth state, which exists only
   because `Rendering.wired` names a template - and §1.3 never models rendering
   variants. **There was nothing in §1.3 to replace.**
3. **PLAN DECISION D3 ALREADY STATES THE RULE THIS WAY, inside the paragraph
   defining `auto`**, and this writer implemented it without noticing: *"A new
   variant `{ kind: "auto" }` is added by Task 8: try every template in the
   registry's order; the first `ok` wins; **all** `not-applicable` selects ELK;
   any `invalid-geometry`, `clearance` or `backend-raised` refuses."* Step 7 of
   the plan then restates it with the `auto` scope dropped. **So the plan
   contradicts itself, and what is implemented is the half D3 holds** - there
   is no question here for the owner to overrule, only a document to make
   self-consistent.

So `selectRenderer` reaches `{kind:"elk"}` only for an `auto` block, and a
wired block's last `not-applicable` becomes a `refused`. Spec §1.3's rules are
unchanged and need no amending; what is written down is the scope D3 already
gave them.

- **Found** 2026-10-19, Task 8, Step 7, as a red suite on the first
  implementation of the rule as the brief states it.
- **Evidence** the plan's own two sentences, quoted above and checkable in
  `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-19-schematic-authoring-m1.md`: **D3's heading
  is line 61 and its `auto` sentence is line 63** (scoped), against its Task 8
  Step 7 at line 809 (unscoped). And the 43 failures, which are
  the **ported** template tests' assertions rather than this task's, so they
  could not have been written to suit the conclusion.
- **AND ROUND 1 CITED A TEST THAT DOES NOT HOLD THE DISTINCTION, WHICH IS ITS
  OWN FINDING.** It said *"the corrected rule is held by
  `tests/schgen/render/selection.test.ts`, whose `auto` fixture selects ELK and
  whose `wired` fixture refuses"*. The wired fixture refused with
  `invalid-geometry`, **which refuses under the unscoped rule too** - so
  deleting the `rendering.kind === "auto"` condition left all four selection
  tests green and only the ported template tests red. Measured in review. A
  fourth case now holds it: *"a declared template that does not apply
  REFUSES; only an auto block falls to ELK"*, a `wired` divider block given the
  T network of `divider.test.ts`, asserting `refused` **and**
  `mismatch.kind === "not-applicable"`. `[RAN]` With the condition deleted it
  fails alone:

  ```
  (fail) selectRenderer > a declared template that does not apply REFUSES; only an auto block falls to ELK
  Expected: "refused"
  Received: "elk"
  ```

  Restored; 5 pass / 0 fail. Step 10's two perturbations removed the whole
  `return { kind: "elk" }` line or rerouted `invalid-geometry`, which are
  different edits testing different things and neither of which discriminates
  this rule.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer wrote the rule both ways, ran the suite
  each time, and ran the condition-deletion perturbation against the new fourth
  test. The three licenses above were RELAYED by the Task 8 reviewer; the D3
  quotation was re-read in the plan before being written down here.
- **THE PLAN'S HALF IS ALREADY CLOSED, BY SOMEONE ELSE.** `[CODE]` Step 7 at
  line 808 now opens *"CORRECTED 2026-10-20 by controller ruling R19 - this
  step contradicted D3 and D3 is right"*, carries D3's scope in both
  directions, and cites this entry. Verified by reading it. **The Task 8 brief
  under `.superpowers/` still states the rule unscoped once**, and that file is
  gitignored, so nothing in the committed tree disagrees with itself any more.
- **Why it is open** not for the plan's sake. It stays because its content is
  what a later task needs and cannot re-derive: **the three licenses** (so
  nobody re-opens the question by reading §1.3 alone and finding no row for
  this state), and **the 43-test measurement** (so nobody re-tries the unscoped
  rule to see what happens). Tasks 9, 10, 12 and 15 are written against this
  rule, and the one place it is stated in code is `selectRenderer`'s comment,
  which is prose beside an implementation - the shape **G132** item 1 objects
  to, since nothing checks that the two still agree.
- **What would settle it** **CRITERION:** the asymmetry is enforced by a check
  rather than described, so a future edit that routes a declared template's
  `not-applicable` to ELK fails by name rather than by 43 tests that are about
  something else. **MECHANISM, done:**
  `tests/schgen/render/selection.test.ts`'s fourth case is that check, and
  deleting the condition fails it alone (above). What remains unchecked, and is
  the residual, is that `selectRenderer`'s canonical comment still matches what
  the function does - no check compares them.

### G148 - `BlockDeclaration.prefixes` is not in Task 9's brief, and the reason is a measured false positive: a composed `Network` does not retain its `include()` prefixes

Plan decision **D1** requires that *"the declared blocks AGREE WITH the
`include()` prefixes wherever a prefix exists"* and forbids the obvious
shortcut in the same breath: *"recovering it by string-prefix matching would put
the cut back in the generator's hands."* Task 9's brief then gives
`BlockDeclaration` six fields, none of which says which prefix a block is.

**`includeNetwork` prefixes a component id with `${prefix}_` and the prefix is
then GONE.** A composed `Network` is a flat list of components whose ids are
plain strings; nothing in it distinguishes `audio_input_coupling_cap`, which
arrived through `include("audio", …)`, from a component somebody simply called
that. So the check D1 asks for is **impossible from the `Network` alone**, and
`BlockDeclaration` gains a seventh field, `prefixes: BlockPrefixes`, holding the
prefixes a block's members come from plus the `why` D1 requires when a block
holds more than one.

**THE DERIVATION THAT LOOKS LIKE IT WOULD WORK, AND THE BOARD IT FAILS ON.**
Taking the longest common `_`-separated prefix of each block's declared members
and then checking that no non-member carries it needs no new field and gets
`optical-compressor` right (`power`, `audio`, `sidechain`) and FOUR of
`transistor-preamp`'s six legs right. **It fails on two of them**, and both
failures are the same shape - a component outside the leg whose id happens to
start with the leg's longest common segment prefix:

| leg | its members | longest common segment prefix | the non-member that breaks it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `collector` | `collector_floor`, `collector_trim` | `collector` | `collector_test_point`, a member of the stage block |
| `emitterBypass` | `emitter_bypass_jumper`, `emitter_bypass_trim` | `emitter_bypass` | `emitter_bypass_cap`, which `Leg` has no slot for and which is declared outside `LEGS`, so it is a member of the stage block |

The derivation therefore reports two D1 violations on a declaration that has
none.

- **Found** 2026-10-20, Task 9, while implementing `blockPrefixDisagreements`.
- **Evidence** `grep -n 'collector_' circuits/transistor-preamp/lab-board.ts`
  returns **five** lines, verbatim:

  ```
  73:    floor: { id: "collector_floor", value: "1k" },
  74:    trimId: "collector_trim", trim: "2k",
  128:    .connector("collector_test_point", { "1": COLLECTOR }, TEST_POINT)
  149:  collector_floor: "R5", collector_trim: "RV5",
  156:  collector_test_point: "TP4", ground_test_point: "TP5", input_test_point: "TP6",
  ```

  Lines 73-74 are the `collector` entry of `LEGS` and line 128 is the test
  point, which is a member of the stage block. The second failure is the same
  grep for `emitter_bypass`: `circuits/transistor-preamp/lab-board.ts` declares
  `emitter_bypass_jumper` and `emitter_bypass_trim` inside `LEGS` and
  `emitter_bypass_cap` outside it, because `Leg` has slots for a jumper, a floor
  resistor and a trim-pot and none for a capacitor. A check that could have
  failed: the legs and these two components could have shared no segment, and
  then the derivation would have been sound - which is what happens for the
  other four legs. `tests/schgen/from-network.test.ts`'s block-prefix cases exercise
  the field in both directions - a component carrying a declared prefix and not
  a member, and a block declaring no prefix holding a component another block's
  prefix claims.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer tried the derivation, found the false
  positive on `collector_test_point`, and wrote the field instead.
- **Why it is open** it is a deviation from a stated interface, recorded so the
  reviewer sees it was a choice rather than drift, and so a later task does not
  delete the field believing the brief's six are the contract.
- **What would settle it** **CRITERION: the check D1 asks for runs, and it
  cannot report a violation on a declaration that has none.** It is met. What
  would make the field unnecessary is **a `Network` that retains its composition
  provenance** - an `include()` that records the prefix on each component it
  moves - which is a change to `lib/model/include.ts` and well outside Task 9.
  **MECHANISM for that, untried:** a `provenance.prefix` on the composed
  component, which `Component.provenance` already has a shape for and which
  `assertSameTopology` already ignores.

### G149 - `SchematicAuthoring.declared` is not in Task 9's brief either: `PartSpec.source` has no source in this model, and `BomFields` has no source for three of its four keys

Two `PartSpec` fields the IR requires have nowhere in the circuit model to come
from, and the brief names neither a field for them nor a rule.

**`source`.** `ir/validate.ts`'s `partShapes` refuses a blank one - *"name the
design-note section or datasheet the part comes from"* - and
`Component.provenance` is set on **0 of the 102 components across the four
parity circuits**. Each circuit's module comment names its own authority in
prose; `declared.source` is that sentence in a field, one per circuit.

**AND THAT IS A GRANULARITY LOSS, named here because the field hides it**
(Task 9 review, round 1, minor M3). `PartSpec.source` is PER PART and
`partShapes` reads it that way - *"the design-note section or datasheet the part
comes from"* - so a 37-component circuit whose spec states a different section
per part collapses to one string. `circuits/optical-compressor/index.ts`'s
`SPEC_NAMES` already carries the per-part sections (*"R_SHUNT (8.3)"*,
*"C_DET (8.6)"*) and nothing reads them. The loss is real and was accepted
because a per-part source map is a fourth declared field for a value no consumer
reads yet; the criterion below covers it.

**`BomFields`, and this is the decision Task 9's brief asked for by name**
(*"either the authoring file declares them or `bomFields` refuses - do not
default them to empty strings and do not widen the exemption list silently.
Decide, implement, and record which"*). The field wants Manufacturer, MPN,
Supplier and SupplierPart. **The model has a slot for exactly one of the four**,
`PartSpec.mpn`, set on 14 of the 102 components. The repository's purchasing data
is real and is keyed the other way round: `parts/*.json` holds a catalog entry
per orderable part with supplier evidence per spec, and `boards/<board>/bom.json`
joins a BOARD's lines to it by a `"<kind> <value> <footprint>"` string. **Two of
the eleven boards have a `bom.json` at all**, and nothing joins a board line to
a circuit model's component.

**THE DECISION, IMPLEMENTED:** `declared.bom` is a `BomSource`, either
`{ kind: "declared", fields }` - per component id, and a component with no entry
refuses by name - or `{ kind: "unsourced", why }`, an explicit declaration
carrying its reason that this circuit has no purchasing data. All four parity
circuits declare `unsourced`. `bomFieldsFor` then returns the four keys empty,
and **the IR's own `bomFields` validation rule refuses every non-exempt part by
name the moment anyone validates the circuit** - which is the brief's *"or
`bomFields` refuses"*. `BOM_EXEMPT_PREFIXES` is untouched and still covers `TP`,
`H` and `FID` and nothing else; `transistor-preamp`'s seven test points are
exempt through it, as they already were.

The three alternatives and why each is worse: blanking the fields with no
declaration is the silent default the brief forbids by name; widening
`BOM_EXEMPT_PREFIXES` makes a live check unable to fail; and writing plausible
manufacturers and supplier part numbers into four authoring files is fabricated
purchasing data, which is worse than none because it looks orderable.

- **Found** 2026-10-20, Task 9, Step 4.
- **Evidence** `bun tools/schgen/authoring-census.ts` builds all four circuits
  and would have reported a `provenance` or `mpn` to read if there were one;
  `find boards -name bom.json` returns two paths
  (`boards/pt2399-core/bom.json`, `boards/transistor-preamp-staged/bom.json`)
  against eleven directories under `boards/`, and
  `boards/pt2399-core/bom.json`'s `lines` object holds one entry, keyed
  `"capacitor .1uF C_Disc_D5.0mm_W2.5mm_P2.50mm"`. `tests/schgen/from-network.test.ts`
  drives the `declared` arm too, which the four circuits do not: a component
  missing from `declared.bom.fields` refuses by name, and one present carries
  its Manufacturer and MPN through to the `PartSpec`.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer read both `bom.json` files, counted the
  `boards/` directories and the provenance/mpn coverage, and implemented and
  tested both arms.
- **Why it is open** it is a deviation from a stated interface plus an owner-
  relevant decision about where purchasing data lives, and the join it names
  does not exist.
- **What would settle it** two criteria. For `source`, **CRITERION: a part's
  `source` names the section or datasheet THAT PART comes from, not only the
  document its circuit comes from** - unmet, and `SPEC_NAMES` is where the data
  for `optical-compressor` already is. For BOM, **CRITERION: a generated
  schematic's BOM fields are either read from this repository's own catalog or
  absent by a declaration that says why - never blank by default.** The first half is unmet and is the
  interesting one. **MECHANISM, untried and this writer has not tried to judge
  it: a join from a circuit model's component to a `parts/*.json` catalog id**,
  which `boards/<board>/bom.json` today spells as a `"<kind> <value>
  <footprint>"` string and which would have to survive a component with no
  footprint (`optical-compressor` has 37 of those - **G152**).

### G150 - measured: 31 nets across two of the four parity circuits are not UPPER_SNAKE, so nothing can turn them into KiCad labels without a rule nobody has written - a SIXTH invention beyond G99's five

`NET_NAME` in `lib/schgen/ir/types.ts` is `/^[A-Z0-9][A-Z0-9_]*$/` and
`ir/validate.ts`'s `netNames` rule refuses anything else. The circuit models do
not meet it:

| circuit | nets | not UPPER_SNAKE | examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `opamp-buffer` | 7 | **0** | |
| `optical-compressor` | 22 | **14** | `+9V_RAW`, `+9V_PROTECTED` (leading `+`); `audio_BUF_OUT`, `sidechain_Q_COLLECTOR` (the `include()` prefix is lower case) |
| `pt2399-core` | 21 | **17** | `+5V`; `Net-(U1-LPF1-IN)` and ten more like it; `unconnected-(U1-CLK_O-Pad5)` |
| `transistor-preamp` | 18 | **0** | |

**NEITHER CAUSE IS AN ACCIDENT AND BOTH ARE LOAD-BEARING WHERE THEY ARE.**
`includeNetwork` writes `${prefix}_${net}` and the prefixes are the lower-case
block names `circuits/optical-compressor/index.ts` composes with; renaming them
would change what `include()` means. `pt2399-core`'s names are transcribed
verbatim from the netlist of a unit that was built and works, and that file says
so: *"Net names are copied verbatim from the netlist, including KiCad's
auto-generated 'Net-(...)' names"*, because the transcription is the authority
for the board.

**WHY IT IS AN INVENTION AND NOT ONLY A VALIDATION FAILURE.** A generated
schematic carries net names as global labels and power-symbol values. Something
between a `Network` and a `.kicad_sch` therefore has to decide what
`Net-(U1-LPF1-IN)` is called on the sheet - and a renaming is not cosmetic,
because the round-trip check spec §2 names (*"export a netlist from the
generated `.kicad_sch` with `kicad-cli` and compare it against the section
network"*) compares net names. **Task 9 invents nothing: `circuitSpecFrom`
passes every net name through verbatim**, which is why this is recorded rather
than fixed.

- **Found** 2026-10-20, Task 9, while measuring the four circuits.
- **Evidence** `netsNotUpperSnake` in `lib/schgen/authoring.ts`, which tests
  every net of a `Network` against the IR's own `NET_NAME` and is printed per
  circuit by `bun tools/schgen/authoring-census.ts` (the figures above are that
  output on 2026-10-20). A check that could have failed: two of the four
  circuits report 0, so the function is not simply reporting everything.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer wrote the measurement, ran it, and read
  the full list of 31 names.
- **Why it is open** it is a real gap in the chain and it is nobody's in the
  current plan: Task 9 declares what a backend needs and net naming is not in
  its brief; the task that writes a `.kicad_sch` is the one that cannot avoid
  it. **G102 is why this entry matters beyond its own content**: it warned that
  G99's list of five inventions was a lower bound because the check behind it
  had a blind spot, and this is the sixth.
- **What would settle it** **CRITERION: every net of a circuit that reaches a
  generated sheet carries a name the IR accepts, and the mapping from the
  model's name to that name is stated once and is reversible** - reversible
  because spec §2's round trip compares the exported netlist against the model.
  **MECHANISMS, untried, and they disagree:** normalise in the generator
  (cheap, and breaks the round trip unless the comparison normalises too);
  declare a per-circuit rename map in the authoring file (explicit, and 31 more
  lines to keep correct); or relax `NET_NAME` (which would admit a name KiCad
  itself quotes differently, and nobody has checked what KiCad does with
  `Net-(U1-REF)` as a global label). The criterion is what binds.

### G151 - a symbol pin the model says nothing about reaches a `CircuitSpec` neither on a net nor declared not-connected, and `ncUnlisted` needs a reason the model cannot hold

`circuits/opamp-buffer.ts` wires one section of a TL072 and says so in its own
header: *"One unit is declared here, for the section that is used. … Note that
section B is simply UNDECLARED - no pin here is an explicit no-connect, and this
circuit authors no `NC`."*

`Amplifier_Operational:TL072` has eight pins across three units. `circuitSpecFrom`
emits `units: [1, 2, 3]` - every unit of the resolved symbol, because
`ir/validate.ts`'s `unitsPlaced` requires every unit to be placed - and declares
pins 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8 from the model's connections. **Pins 5, 6 and 7 are
declared nowhere.** The IR's `pinsDeclared` rule then refuses them by name:
*"pin 5 (+) is neither on a net nor declared not connected"*.

**`ncUnlisted` IS THE FIELD FOR EXACTLY THIS AND IT CANNOT BE SET HERE.** Its
shape is `{ reason: string }` - *"Explicit opt-in … The reason is required"* -
and the circuit model has nowhere to put a reason. `from-network.ts` therefore
emits `null` and invents no no-connect, which is the right refusal and leaves
the circuit un-validatable until something declares the intent.

- **Found** 2026-10-20, Task 9, Step 4, from `opamp-buffer.ts`'s own header.
- **Evidence** the TL072's unit and pin counts read through
  `createResolver(symbolLibraries(["Amplifier_Operational"])).resolve("Amplifier_Operational:TL072")`
  - 8 pins, 3 units, pins 5 (`+`, unit 2), 6 (`-`, unit 2) and 7 (output, unit
  2) - against `opamp-buffer.ts`, which declares one unit named "A" with three
  pins plus the two package pins. **A check that could have failed, added by the Task 9
  review's round 1:** `tests/schgen/authoring-complete.test.ts` now runs
  `validateCircuit` on all four circuits and asserts the exact refusal counts
  per rule class, of which `pinsDeclared` is **3 on `opamp-buffer` and 0 on the
  other three** - pins 5, 6 and 7 of U1, by name. The earlier version of this
  entry said the gap was invisible to the suite; that was true when it was
  written and is no longer.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer resolved the symbol, read its pins, and
  read the circuit's declaration and its header sentence.
- **Why it is open** it needs either a model change (somewhere to say "this
  section is unused, and why") or an authoring-file field, and neither is in
  Task 9's brief. It is also NOT only `opamp-buffer`'s: any circuit that wires
  one section of a multi-section package has it.
- **What would settle it** **CRITERION: a symbol pin that no part of the model
  connects is either declared not-connected with a stated reason, or the
  generator refuses naming the pin - and the suite exercises one of the two.**
  **MECHANISM, untried:** a `ncUnlisted` entry in `ComponentOverride`, which
  keeps the reason beside the other claims the authoring file makes; the
  competing one is to let the model declare an unused unit, which is the better
  home and the larger change.

### G152 - measured: `optical-compressor` declares a footprint on 0 of its 37 components, and an empty footprint field is not checked by anything

`PartSpec.footprint` in the IR is a required `string`. `PartSpec.footprint` in
the circuit model is optional, and `circuits/optical-compressor/` sets it on
**none** of its 37 components, deliberately: `parts/inert-terminal.ts` states
*"No footprint and no mpn: the spec names the connectors and their pins and says
nothing about packaging, and inventing either would be fabricated data."*

`from-network.ts` carries that absence across as `""`, which is the faithful
transcription of a stated absence and an ordinary legal state in a KiCad
schematic. **What is worth recording is that nothing downstream objects.**
`ir/validate.ts`'s rule set checks a part's label, refPrefix, source, units,
pins, BOM fields and mechanical pads; **there is no footprint rule at all**, so
an empty footprint passes validation in silence. The other three circuits
declare a footprint on every component, so the condition exists on exactly one
of the four and only there.

- **Found** 2026-10-20, Task 9, Step 4.
- **Evidence** `bun tools/schgen/authoring-census.ts` builds each circuit and a
  companion sweep over `component.part?.footprint` reports 0 of 37 for
  `optical-compressor` and full coverage for the other three (9 of 9, 24 of 24,
  32 of 32). `grep -n 'footprint' lib/schgen/ir/validate.ts
  lib/schgen/ir/validate-parts.ts lib/schgen/ir/validate-nets.ts` returns
  **exactly one line**, and it is a COMMENT:

  ```
  lib/schgen/ir/validate-parts.ts:50:      // No schematic construct carries a net on a footprint pad that has no symbol pin.
  ```

  No rule reads `IrPart.footprint` at all. That one line is the check that
  could have failed - a real footprint rule would have matched the same grep -
  and reading it as a rule is the mistake this entry exists to prevent.
- **Verified** CONFIRMED - this writer ran both the sweep and the grep and read
  their output.
- **Why it is open** it is a measurement plus a silent-pass, not a defect in
  Task 9's work. An empty footprint is correct for a schematic and wrong for
  anything that lays out a board, and the thing that will care is whichever task
  takes a generated schematic toward a PCB or a BOM.
- **What would settle it** **CRITERION: a part reaching an artifact that needs a
  footprint either has one or is refused by name; a part reaching a drawing that
  does not need one is not refused for lacking it.** Those are two different
  consumers and one rule in `validateCircuit` cannot serve both, which is why
  this is recorded rather than fixed by adding a rule. **MECHANISM, untried:** a
  rule outside `validateCircuit`, run by the consumers that need footprints.

### G153 - measured: all 51 interface ports the four circuits declare are `negotiable` and none is `fixed`, because no block declares a template - so seam B has maximum freedom and nothing to honour

Spec §1.9 asks a block to declare *"which attachment positions are FIXED and
which are NEGOTIABLE"*, where fixed means *"a position fixed by the block's own
internal geometry"*, and §1.9 deliberately leaves to the seam B task *"how a
fixed position is distinguished from a negotiable one in a particular block"*.

**Task 9's four declarations contain no fixed position at all, and the reason is
structural rather than a shortcut.** Every one of the twelve declared blocks is
`{ kind: "auto" }`: no circuit declares a reviewed template on any block,
because declaring one is choosing an arrangement and Task 9 has no criterion for
that choice. A block with no template has no internal geometry yet, so there is
nothing for a position to be fixed BY.

| circuit | blocks | interface ports | fixed | negotiable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `opamp-buffer` | 1 | 5 | 0 | 5 |
| `optical-compressor` | 3 | 17 (4 + 7 + 6) | 0 | 17 |
| `pt2399-core` | 1 | 6 | 0 | 6 |
| `transistor-preamp` | 7 | 23 (2+2+2+2+2+4+9) | 0 | 23 |
| **total** | **12** | **51** | **0** | **51** |

**THIS IS THE FIRST MEASUREMENT OF WHAT G100's MISSING 43 EDGES COST.** G100
measured `optical-compressor` at 139 edges drawn whole against 96 in its three
blocks, and the spec review found §1.9 by asking where the other 43 went:
*"they became block-interface connections - legitimate, but they must be
represented when blocks are composed."* The representation now exists and that
circuit's three blocks declare **17** interface ports for it. 17 ports is not 43
edges and the two numbers are not comparable without care: an edge in G100's
count is a net-to-pin incidence in an ELK graph and a port here is a NET, so one
port stands for as many edges as it has pins on either side of the cut.

**AND THE SIDES ARE A DECLARATION THIS TASK MADE, recorded so it can be
disputed.** §1.9 also leaves *"which sides are acceptable for which kind of
port"* open. `negotiablePort` in `lib/schgen/authoring.ts` is the sentence the
four files declare by calling it, built from two things already in the tree: a
rail attaches where `RailSpec`'s own doc comment says its glyph goes (*"ground
rails are drawn at the bottom of blocks with downward symbols; supplies at the
top"*), and everything else attaches left for `in`, right for `out` and either
for `bidirectional` or for a crossing net with no declared direction, because
plan decision **D4** pins flow left-to-right. It is a helper the authoring files
call, never a rule the generator applies - an interface §1.9 says is declared
cannot be derived by the thing that reads it.

- **Found** 2026-10-20, Task 9, Step 6.
- **Evidence** `bun tools/schgen/authoring-census.ts`, whose per-block line
  prints members, interface ports and the fixed/negotiable split; the table
  above is that output on 2026-10-20. A check that could have failed:
  `tests/schgen/from-network.test.ts` drives a `fixed` port with a non-blank
  `why` through `authoringProblems` and finds no problem, and the same port with
  a blank `why` refuses - so "0 fixed" is a property of the four declarations
  and not of a `fixed` arm that does not work.
